script: New York bought the Moon with a borrowed glass. Plates sit empty while the clock slams toward print. Richard Adams Locke sees the paper’s trust on the line. The Sun must fill a sky tonight or fail. How? Richard Adams Locke sets a line that cites the Edinburgh Journal of Science. He prints bat-winged people and busy beavers on craters. Then he promises six parts to drip the news. Then the letters arrive. Sir John Herschel, at the Cape, denies any part. That journal ended in 1833, yet the name sells. Reprints race the claim across city after city. Yet readers ask if any of this is real. The Sun hints fiction inside, skips a front apology. Here are the Sun pages and that bold line. Here is Herschel’s own letter saying no. People trust a voice that sounds like science. Richard Adams Locke and the team didn’t sell the Moon at all. New York kept its Moon with a borrowed name.
